claude_take: A theme runs through today's stories: whoever already holds leverage keeps getting the benefit of the doubt, while everyone else gets the fine print. Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang days after his resignation over an espionage scandal, reportedly under direct White House pressure, with its own security review still unresolved; Denmark's top court sided with the state's "ghetto law" despite an EU finding that it may be discriminatory; and UK actors won real AI protections from producers but couldn't close the gap that matters most — stopping their old work from training the models that might replace them. Underneath all of it, the economic anxiety none of these deals actually touch keeps surfacing from below, from Gucci cutting Swiss jobs to tens of thousands marching in Paris five months before an election built on exactly that anger.
claude_take_title: Leverage Gets the Benefit of the Doubt

items.headline: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Just Days After His Resignation
items.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO on November 23, less than two weeks after he resigned amid reports of an affair with a person US officials suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. The board said it had received input from senior US government officials and was confident his return poses no national security risk, even though its independent review of the matter is still ongoing. Nvidia shares jumped more than 31% on the news, and CNN reported the reversal followed direct pressure from President Trump and the White House; Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott has scheduled Huang to testify publicly in December.

items.headline: CrowdStrike to Acquire Zscaler for $43.9 Billion in All-Stock Deal
items.summary: CrowdStrike announced on November 23 that it will acquire network-security rival Zscaler in an all-stock transaction valuing the company at roughly $43.9 billion, with Zscaler shareholders receiving 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share held. The deal, disclosed alongside CrowdStrike's fiscal third-quarter results, pushes the endpoint-security leader into network security, which it calls cybersecurity's largest single market segment, as both companies race to secure the AI agents increasingly operating inside corporate systems. The transaction is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year ending January 2028 and carries a $1.4 billion termination fee if it falls through.

items.headline: Netflix's First-Ever IMAX Release Opens Without Regal or Cinemark
items.summary: David Fincher's "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," a Quentin Tarantino-scripted continuation of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" starring Brad Pitt, opens November 25 as Netflix's first film ever released in IMAX, playing exclusively in theaters for two weeks before streaming December 23. Regal and Cinemark have both declined to show it on their IMAX screens, with Cinemark's CEO saying the arrangement isn't "constructive" for the theatrical ecosystem, leaving AMC's roughly 500 IMAX screens worldwide to carry most of the release. The standoff is the latest flashpoint in theater chains' uneasy, case-by-case accommodation of Netflix's short theatrical windows.

items.headline: UK Actors Secure First Collective AI Rights, but Gaps Remain
items.summary: Equity, the UK performers' union, and producers' body Pact have reached a landmark three-year deal giving British actors their first collective rights over AI digital replicas, requiring producers to get consent and pay performers before creating or using a digital double, and barring replica use during disputes. Members are voting on the deal, which also includes a 24% pay rise for film work, through a ballot closing November 30, with union leadership recommending a yes. Equity has acknowledged the agreement does not clearly stop performers' past work from being used to train AI systems, the gap most likely to resurface when talks on that issue resume in January.

items.headline: Tens of Thousands March in Paris as Cost-of-Living Protests Stretch Toward France's Election
items.summary: Tens of thousands marched in Paris on November 23, with similar demonstrations in Rome, Spain, Portugal, Germany and the UK, in the latest of a weekslong wave of French protests over the cost of living, public-service cuts and political gridlock. Organizers and reporting increasingly frame the unrest around France's presidential election in five months, where a far-right party sees its best opening yet to capitalize on the anger. The protests have run for several consecutive weekends, drawing anywhere from roughly 100,000 to over 600,000 people nationwide on different dates, with no sign of losing momentum heading into the vote.

items.headline: Denmark's Top Court Upholds Housing Law Targeting 'Non-Western' Residents
items.summary: Denmark's Supreme Court ruled on November 23 against seven former tenants of a Helsingør housing estate who argued their leases were terminated on discriminatory grounds under the country's so-called "ghetto law," which sets lower redevelopment thresholds for estates with large shares of residents from "non-Western" backgrounds. The ruling upholds the hardline law even though the EU's top court found in December 2025 that it may amount to ethnic discrimination, since EU preliminary rulings guide but don't bind national courts on the final outcome. The decision effectively lets Denmark keep using ethnicity-linked housing thresholds as an integration-policy tool, a model other European governments have watched closely.

items.headline: Gucci's Watch Division Cuts 30 Jobs in Switzerland, Shifts Work to Italy
items.summary: Gucci Swiss Timepieces, the watchmaking arm of Kering-owned Gucci, is cutting about 30 of the roughly 95 jobs at its Cortaillod, Switzerland manufacturing site, with the brand relocating logistics operations to its facility in Trecate, Italy. Kering confirmed the cuts to AFP after they were first reported by a local Neuchâtel radio station, part of a broader pullback across Swiss watchmaking as the industry grapples with falling exports and Gucci's own push to focus on higher-end timepieces. The move follows a smaller round of 21 cuts at the same division last year and comes as rival Zenith, owned by LVMH, separately cuts about 100 jobs at its nearby Le Locle factory.

items.headline: Epicurus's Tetrapharmakos
items.summary: Epicurus distilled his philosophy into a "four-part cure" for anxiety: don't fear the gods, don't fear death, what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure. He argued that most human suffering comes not from pain itself but from needless dread about things we cannot actually experience or that pass quickly once faced directly — death, in particular, is "nothing to us" because we cease to exist before we could ever suffer it. The goal was ataraxia, a tranquil freedom from disturbance achieved through modest pleasures, friendship and clear thinking rather than wealth or status. The idea still underpins much of modern stress-reduction and stoic-adjacent self-help, even when it drops Epicurus's name entirely.
items.summary_fr: Épicure a résumé sa philosophie en un « quadruple remède » contre l'angoisse : ne pas craindre les dieux, ne pas craindre la mort, le bien est facile à obtenir, et le mal est facile à supporter. Il soutenait que la plupart des souffrances humaines ne viennent pas de la douleur elle-même, mais d'une crainte inutile de choses qu'on ne peut en réalité jamais vivre ou qui s'estompent dès qu'on les affronte clairement — la mort, en particulier, n'est « rien pour nous » puisque nous cessons d'exister avant de pouvoir jamais en souffrir. Le but était l'ataraxie, une tranquillité de l'âme obtenue par des plaisirs simples, l'amitié et une pensée claire plutôt que par la richesse ou le statut social. Cette idée irrigue encore une grande partie du développement personnel contemporain, même quand on a oublié jusqu'au nom d'Épicure.
